summary: Open with a small bitcoin position of $250 and keep the other three quarters in cash, because bitcoin is in a falling trend and is resting on a long-term support line that may or may not hold.
thesis:
Bitcoin closed 11 November at $73,928 and was trading near $73,500 to $73,700 around the time of this decision. It is down about 16% from its September peak and roughly 7% over the past month. It sits below its 20-day average (about $78,100) and its 50-day average (about $81,400), and only about 1% above its 200-day average (about $73,100), which it briefly broke on Tuesday. By the plan's own test, bitcoin below its recent average and falling, this is a time to hold less.

The reasons behind the fall have not gone away. October US consumer prices rose 0.4% on the month, more than expected, and futures now put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December at roughly 85% to 95%. Higher interest rates usually weigh on assets like crypto. US spot bitcoin funds have lost money on most days this month, about $1.3 billion in the first week alone, and the largest fund had seven straight days of withdrawals to 9 November. Sentiment gauges read fear (Fear and Greed index in the high 20s), and reports say small investors are not buying the dip.

There are two reasons not to sit entirely in cash. First, the account is measured against simply holding bitcoin, so owning none is itself a large bet. Second, the price is at a level where long-term buyers have often stepped in, the pace of fund withdrawals has slowed (from $412 million on Friday to $201 million on Monday), and fearful sentiment tends to come late in a decline rather than early. A quarter of the account in bitcoin keeps me in the game if the line holds and limits the damage if it does not.

I am not buying other coins. Ether, Solana and XRP have all fallen more than bitcoin over the past month (Solana about 19% and below its own 200-day average), ether funds are also seeing withdrawals, and none has a specific reason of its own that would justify the extra risk right now.

What I will do next: add to bitcoin, and consider ether, if bitcoin closes back above about $75,500 and then its 20-day average with fund flows turning positive. Hold at this size while it drifts between about $72,000 and $75,500. Cut the position if bitcoin posts daily closes clearly below about $72,000, which would mean the 200-day line has failed. This view is wrong if bitcoin rebounds sharply from here, in which case I will lag the benchmark and pay up to rejoin.
risks: If bitcoin bounces hard off its 200-day average, three quarters of the account in cash will fall behind the benchmark. If the line breaks, the $250 position loses money, though far less than a full holding would. The fill is at the 13 November open, which could differ noticeably from today's price. The averages and fund-flow figures come from news reports rather than my own calculation and may be slightly off. The Fed decision on 9 December and inflation data on 25 November could move prices sharply either way.
strategy_change: Plan moved to version 2. It now names the measures of trend (the 20-day, 50-day and 200-day averages of bitcoin's price) and sets rough exposure bands: about 0-30% invested when bitcoin is below both shorter averages, about 30-60% once it is back above the 20-day average, and up to fully invested when it is above both and rising. It also notes that the 35% limit per holding means matching bitcoin in an uptrend requires holding other coins, with ether as the default second holding.

orders.reason: Starter anchor position, about 25% of the account, at the 200-day average while the shorter trend is still down.

summary: Open the account three quarters invested: $300 in an S&P 500 fund, $300 in an equal-weight S&P 500 fund and $150 in a health care fund, keeping $250 in cash until Nvidia's results and the December interest rate decision are out of the way.
thesis:
This is the first trade. The account starts with $1,000 in cash and the plan says to stay mostly invested with a broad core.

The backdrop is mixed. The S&P 500 fund SPY ended 11 November at $759.81, about 4% above its 200-day average ($731) but just under its 50-day average ($765) and roughly flat over one and three months. Under that calm surface a lot has moved. Technology and chip stocks have fallen hard (XLK down 8.4% and the chip fund SMH down 10.2% over 20 trading days) while health care, banks, consumer staples and the average stock have risen (XLV up 8.6%, XLF up 7.5%, and the equal-weight fund RSP up 5.0% over the same 20 days). RSP is above its 20, 50 and 200-day averages; SPY and the Nasdaq fund QQQ are below their 50-day averages.

Three things are pushing in that direction. First, inflation: October consumer prices rose 0.4% against 0.3% expected, the 10-year Treasury yield is at about 5%, and markets put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December at roughly 86% to 88%, with one Fed governor saying a larger increase should be considered. Higher rates hurt the most expensive stocks most. Second, the largest company in the index has a leadership crisis: Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into its chief executive and is reported to be weighing whether to remove him, the shares were down more than 5% before the open today, and its results are expected around 18 November. Third, the recovery in chip stocks this week has won back less than a third of what they lost since early October. Futures on the morning of 12 November pointed to the S&P 500 opening about 0.4% lower and the Nasdaq 100 about 0.8% lower.

What I am doing about it:

1. SPY, $300 (30%). The plain core. Proved wrong, and cut, if SPY ends a day below its 200-day average (about $731), which would say the long rise has broken.

2. RSP, $300 (30%). This fund holds the same 500 companies in equal amounts, so it has far less riding on Nvidia and the other giant technology companies than SPY does. It is the main way this account differs from the benchmark: a bet that the average company keeps doing better than the giants while rates rise and the AI trade is in doubt. Proved wrong if RSP ends a day below its 50-day average (about $215), or if over the next month it trails SPY by more than 3 percentage points while technology recovers above its own 50-day average. In either case I would move it into SPY.

3. XLV, $150 (15%). Health care has the strongest trend of any sector on the watchlist (up 11.3% in 60 days, above all three averages) and investors have been using it as shelter from the technology sell-off. It has already run a long way, 18% above its 200-day average, which is why this is half the size of the other two. Proved wrong if XLV falls more than 8% from the purchase price or ends a day below its 50-day average (about $174), or if a concrete change in US drug pricing or insurance policy undercuts the sector.

4. Cash, about $250 (25%). The plan says cash needs a reason and an end date. The reason: within four weeks there is a likely rate increase with a real chance of a larger one, a possible change of chief executive at the index's biggest company, and that company's results. Buying everything on one morning ahead of all three is not needed. The end date: the rest goes into the market no later than the first trading day after the Fed decision of 9 December, and sooner if Nvidia's results pass and SPY is back above its 50-day average. I am leaving this in plain cash because moving it into a Treasury bill fund and back would cost about as much in fees as the interest earned over four weeks.

I considered bank and consumer staples funds, which are also rising, but RSP already holds them and a first portfolio does not need more than three lines. I considered waiting a day because of the weak futures; a 0.4% lower open is a slightly better price, not a reason to stay out. Weekly jobless claims were due after this was written and are not reflected here.

This is the first decision of the month but there is no earlier month on the books, so there is no monthly review; the first is due at the start of December.
risks: If technology and chip stocks rebound sharply, for example on good Nvidia results or a quick settlement of its leadership question, SPY will beat this account because RSP, XLV and cash all hold less technology. Health care has risen a lot in a short time and could give back several percent quickly if the money sheltering there leaves. A rate increase larger than expected, or the 10-year yield moving well above 5%, would likely pull down everything held here, and smaller companies inside RSP are more sensitive to borrowing costs than the giants. Holding 25% in cash loses ground to the benchmark if the market simply rises from here. Prices are from the close of 11 November; the orders fill at today's open, which may differ.

orders.reason: Broad core holding; the long rise is intact with the price about 4% above its 200-day average.
Same 500 companies in equal amounts, so much less depends on Nvidia and giant technology stocks; above all its averages and leading SPY over the past month.
Strongest sector trend and a shelter from the technology sell-off; kept to half size because it has already risen a long way.

summary: No new orders today: bitcoin fell about 3% to around $71,500 to $72,000 and slipped under its 200-day average, so the account stays at the single $250 bitcoin purchase already on its way and keeps the rest in cash.
thesis:
Bitcoin's last price of 11 November was $73,928. During 12 November it fell to between roughly $71,200 and $72,000, its lowest since August, and was near $71,600 in the early evening UTC. That puts it below its 20-day average ($77,705), its 50-day average ($81,120) and now also about 2% below its 200-day average ($73,116), the long-term line it was resting on yesterday. Ether dipped under $2,000, and Solana, XRP and the other large coins fell 3% to 5%.

Several things hit on the same day. Nvidia said its chief executive had left with immediate effect and its shares fell about 13%, dragging down technology shares and crypto with them. The index provider MSCI said it will remove Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, from its main indices at the end of November, which forces index funds to sell that company's shares. US spot bitcoin funds lost about $300 million on 11 November, the fifth straight day of withdrawals and about $1.44 billion in total, and ether funds lost about $145 million. More than $650 million of borrowed bets on rising prices were forcibly closed. Behind all of it, October inflation was higher than expected and markets put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December at about 90%. The supply of dollar-pegged stablecoins, a rough gauge of money waiting to buy crypto, has shrunk by about $14 billion in a month.

What I can and cannot do today. Yesterday's $250 bitcoin purchase has not been made yet: it is made at the first price of 13 November, and the rules do not allow an order to be withdrawn. A sell order sent today would be handled at that same moment, before the purchase, when there is nothing yet to sell, so it would simply be turned away. The real choice today is therefore whether to add, and the plan says no. With bitcoin below both shorter averages and now under the 200-day average, the plan calls for the bottom of its 0-30% range. The purchase on its way is about 25% of the account, already near the top of that range, so I am adding nothing, in bitcoin or anything else. One small comfort is that the purchase will be made roughly 3% cheaper than the price at which I decided on it.

No other coin earns a place. Every coin on the watch list is below its 20-day and 50-day averages, most have fallen further than bitcoin over the past month, and none has news of its own strong enough to outweigh that.

What happens next. Yesterday I said I would cut the position if bitcoin ended its days clearly below about $72,000. Today is ending right around that level, which is a warning but not yet a clear break. If 13 November also ends below about $72,000, I expect to sell at least half of the position in tomorrow's decision, and all of it if the price is heading toward the August low near $69,300. If instead bitcoin climbs back above its 200-day average near $73,100 and holds there, I keep the position, and I still need to see it above about $75,500 with money returning to the bitcoin funds before adding. Doing nothing today is wrong if this was a one-day panic and bitcoin snaps back sharply, in which case three quarters of the account in cash falls behind simply holding bitcoin.
risks: The $250 purchase goes ahead at the first price of 13 November into a falling market, and if the slide continues it will be showing a loss by the time I can sell, though a loss on a quarter of the account is far smaller than the loss on holding bitcoin outright. If the market rebounds hard, the cash will lag the benchmark. US producer price figures on 13 November and a Federal Reserve speech on 14 November could move prices sharply either way. Today's prices come from news reports published between about 14:30 and 18:30 UTC, not from the exchange itself, and the price at midnight UTC may differ.

summary: No new orders: all three holdings are still inside the limits set when they were bought, and the $249 in cash stays put until Nvidia reports on Tuesday, now without a permanent chief executive, and while long-term interest rates are still climbing.
thesis:
The account is one day old. Yesterday's orders filled at the open: about $300 each in the S&P 500 fund SPY and the equal-weight fund RSP, $150 in the health care fund XLV, and $249 left in cash. At the end of 12 November the account was worth $995.61 against $996.46 for the benchmark; most of the gap is the cost of the three purchases.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Nvidia's chief executive resigned on Thursday morning after the reports that led to the board's investigation, and the finance chief is running the company for now. The shares fell as much as 14% at the open and ended the day down about 4%. Results are due on Tuesday 17 November. This is the event the last decision was partly waiting for, and it is not over: the company reports in two trading days with no permanent leader.
- Long-term interest rates rose again. The 10-year Treasury yield went from about 5% to roughly 5.1% on Thursday and was quoted near 5.16% on Friday morning, with oil higher after the President signalled no early end to the Iran war. Two Federal Reserve officials said more tightening is likely to be needed.
- Wholesale prices for October, published this morning, rose 0.3% against 0.4% expected, a slightly better number than feared, though the yearly rate is still 6.5%. Weekly jobless claims on Thursday were 200,000, a little above the 195,000 forecast and still low.
- The S&P 500 fell about 0.4% on Thursday. In early trading on Friday it was close to flat while the index of smaller companies was down more than 1.5%.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. SPY ended 12 November at $757.12. The condition for cutting it is a day ending below its 200-day average, now about $731.60. It is 3.5% above that. Keep.

2. RSP ended at $220.72, down 0.87% on the day against 0.35% for SPY, so it lost a little ground on its first day. The condition for moving it into SPY is a day ending below its 50-day average, now about $215, or trailing SPY by more than 3 percentage points over a month while technology recovers. Neither is close: it is 2.7% above the 50-day average and technology is still well below its own. The thing to watch is that rising long-term rates hurt smaller and more indebted companies most, which is why the small-company index is weak this morning, and RSP holds more of those than SPY does. One day of that does not break the idea. Keep.

3. XLV ended at $187.83, down 0.59% on the day and about 1.3% below what I paid. The conditions for selling are a fall of more than 8% from the purchase price, a day ending below the 50-day average (about $174.70), or a concrete policy change on drug prices or insurance. None has happened and I found no such policy news. Keep.

4. Cash, $249 (25%). The reason for holding it has become stronger in one respect and no weaker in any: Nvidia's leadership question has turned into an actual vacancy days before results, and rates moved up. The end date is unchanged: this money goes into the market no later than the first trading day after the Federal Reserve decision of 9 December, and sooner if Nvidia's results pass and SPY is back above its 50-day average (about $764.80).

I considered putting some of the cash to work in bank or consumer staples funds, which are holding up, and decided against it because RSP already holds them and nothing has changed since yesterday to make a fourth line worth the trading cost. I also considered trimming RSP because of the rate move; the plan says to sell when the reason for holding breaks, and it has not.

A note on timing: this was written after the stock market opened on Friday, later than intended, so any order placed now would have filled at Monday's open. That did not affect the decision, since there are no orders.
risks: If Nvidia's results on Tuesday are well received and technology rebounds, the benchmark will beat this account, which holds less technology and has a quarter in cash. If long-term interest rates keep rising, RSP is likely to fall more than SPY because it holds more smaller, rate-sensitive companies, and it could reach its 50-day average quickly. Health care has risen a long way and could give back several percent if money that sheltered there moves back to technology. Holding cash loses ground whenever the market simply rises. Prices here are from the end of 12 November plus early readings on 13 November, which can change by the end of the day.

summary: Sell the whole bitcoin position and go back to all cash: bitcoin fell to about $68,700, its lowest since August and well under the $72,000 level I said would make me cut, so the condition for selling has been met.
thesis:
Where the account stands. The $250 bitcoin purchase decided on 12 November was made at the first price of 13 November, about $71,400. It does not appear in the account figures yet because those are only updated after the UTC day ends. At around $68,700 the holding is worth about $241, a loss of roughly $9 or 4% on the position and under 1% of the account. The other $750 is cash.

What happened today. Bitcoin's last price of 12 November was $71,370. In the first hours of 13 November it dropped through $70,000 and touched about $67,555 on Coinbase, its lowest price since mid-August, before recovering to between roughly $68,700 and $69,800 during the US day. Reports put it near $68,750 in the late afternoon UTC. The fall was sharpened by forced selling: between $1.3 billion and $1.6 billion of borrowed bets were closed out in 24 hours, almost nine tenths of them bets on rising prices. Ether fell to about $1,930, Solana to about $80 and XRP to about $1.02.

The trend. Bitcoin is now about 11% below its 20-day average ($77,220), 15% below its 50-day average ($80,860) and about 6% below its 200-day average ($73,080), the long-term line it was sitting on two days ago. It is down about 12% over 20 days. Under the plan, prices below both shorter averages and clearly below the 200-day average call for the very bottom of the 0-30% range.

The background has not improved. US spot bitcoin funds had a sixth straight day of withdrawals on 12 November (reports differ on the size, from about $48 million to $284 million), taking the run to roughly $1.5 billion. US producer prices for October rose 0.3% on the month, slightly less than feared, but the yearly rate of 6.5% is the highest since late 2022, and futures still price a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December as close to certain. The dollar is near a 19-month high and the 10-year US government bond yield is around 5.15%, both of which tend to weigh on crypto. Trading is thin, so moves in either direction are exaggerated.

Why sell rather than wait. Yesterday I wrote that I would sell at least half if 13 November ended below about $72,000, and all of it if the price was heading toward the August low near $69,300. The price went through both levels. The runbook says that when a stated condition for selling is met, I sell, and asked fresh whether I would buy bitcoin today under this plan, the answer is no: the plan buys strength and this is weakness. I am selling all of it rather than half because the position is small either way, and a half-measure would mostly be a way of avoiding the decision.

The honest case against selling. This is exactly the sort of moment when prices often bounce. The Fear and Greed index is at 20, its lowest since July; the cost of holding borrowed bets has turned negative, meaning traders are leaning toward further falls; a large flush of forced selling has just happened; and the price is sitting on its 200-week average near $67,750, a level where long-term buyers have stepped in before. A sharp rebound from here is quite possible and I would miss it. I accept that because the plan's working assumption is that trends persist, and I would rather test that assumption cleanly than abandon it on the first hard day. The cost of being wrong is small: buying back in costs about 0.3% plus whatever the price has risen.

No other coin earns a place. Every coin on the watch list is below its 20-day and 50-day averages, most have fallen further than bitcoin over the past month, and none has news of its own.

What would bring me back. I will buy bitcoin again if it ends a UTC day back above its 200-day average, near $73,100, or earlier with a smaller amount if it holds above $70,000 for two UTC days while the bitcoin funds start taking in money again. If instead it falls further, the next levels others are watching are about $64,100 (the 19 August low) and about $60,000; I would not buy just because the price is lower, only once it stops falling and turns.
risks: The main risk is selling near a short-term low: fear is extreme and forced selling has just cleared out many borrowed bets, so a rebound could start at any time, and with no bitcoin at all the account would fall behind the benchmark quickly. The sale is made at the first price of 14 November, which could be noticeably above or below today's levels; weekend trading is thin and can move sharply. A Federal Reserve speech on 14 November, inflation data on 25 November and the rate decision on 9 December could each move prices either way. Today's prices come from news reports published up to the late afternoon UTC, not from the exchange itself, and reports disagree on the size of the fund withdrawals.

orders.reason: Bitcoin broke below $72,000 and the August low near $69,300, the conditions set yesterday for selling; the trend is down on every measure in the plan.

summary: No orders today: the account stays entirely in cash because bitcoin kept falling, to about $65,000 to $66,000, and none of the conditions I set for buying back has been met.
thesis:
Where the account stands. Yesterday's decision to sell the whole bitcoin position was carried out at the first price of 14 November, close to $68,200. The published account figures will show this once the UTC day ends. By my own arithmetic the sale brought in about $238.50, so the account is now roughly $988 in cash and nothing else, about 1.2% below where it started. A plain $1,000 bitcoin holding bought on 11 November would be worth roughly $890 at today's prices.

What happened today. Bitcoin's last price of 13 November was $68,237. During 14 November it slid further, touching about $65,000, its lowest since 19 August, and was reported between roughly $64,200 and $65,800 through the afternoon UTC. That is a further fall of about 4% in a day and about 13% in a week. It also took bitcoin below its 200-week average, near $67,750, a very long-term line that buyers defended yesterday. Ether fell to about $1,840, XRP slipped under $1, and Solana and ether are each down about 18% on the week. More than $1.2 billion of borrowed bets were forcibly closed in 24 hours, about four fifths of them bets on rising prices.

The trend. Using the figures collected for this account, bitcoin at about $65,700 is roughly 14% below its 20-day average ($76,593), 18% below its 50-day average ($80,537) and 10% below its 200-day average ($73,034). Every coin on the watch list is below its own 20-day and 50-day averages. Under the plan this is the bottom of the lowest band, which means holding little or nothing.

The background. US spot bitcoin funds lost about $185 million on 13 November, the seventh straight day of withdrawals and about $1.9 billion over that run. The 10-year US government bond yield is above 5.1%, and markets still expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates on 9 December. None of the pressures that started this fall has eased.

The case for buying, taken seriously. The Fear and Greed index is at 13, its lowest since 1 July. One widely followed analyst describes this as a 'deep value' zone last seen in February and June, where people who bought gradually have done well in the past, while saying plainly that it does not mean the low is in. Forced selling has cleared out many borrowed bets. All of that makes a sharp bounce possible. But each of those points was also true yesterday at $68,700, and the price is 4% lower today. Cheap and frightened are not the same as turning, and this plan buys once the price turns, not while it is still falling. I also set my conditions yesterday precisely so that I would not talk myself into buying on a day like this.

No other coin earns a place. The other coins have fallen further than bitcoin this week and none has news of its own that outweighs the trend.

What would bring me back, unchanged from yesterday. I will buy bitcoin again if it ends a UTC day back above its 200-day average, near $73,000, or earlier with a smaller amount if it holds above $70,000 for two UTC days while the bitcoin funds start taking in money again. I will also watch whether it climbs back above the 200-week average near $67,750 and stays there, as an early sign the fall is ending, though that alone is not enough to buy. Below here, the levels others are watching are about $64,100 (the 19 August low), about $60,000 and about $57,700 (the 1 July low). A lower price by itself is not a reason to buy. This view is wrong if bitcoin rebounds quickly from here: the account would then give back part of its lead over simply holding bitcoin and would buy back in at a higher price.
risks: The main risk is missing a rebound. Fear is extreme, a lot of forced selling has already happened, and weekend trading is thin, so prices can jump as easily as they fall; with no bitcoin at all, the account gains nothing from a bounce and my conditions mean I would buy back several percent above today's price. Holding cash for a long time could also leave the account behind if the market recovers in a slow grind without ever giving a clean signal. Today's prices come from news reports published during the day, which differ from one another by a thousand dollars or more, not from the exchange itself. My estimate of the sale proceeds is my own arithmetic and the official figure may differ slightly. Inflation data on 25 November and the Federal Reserve decision on 9 December could move prices sharply either way.

summary: No new orders: the three holdings are all inside the limits set when they were bought and the account is slightly ahead of its benchmark, so the $249 in cash waits one more day for Nvidia's results on Tuesday evening rather than being spent into a falling chip market the morning before.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Friday 13 November it was worth $995.92 against $992.84 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. The small lead comes from holding less technology: on Friday the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 0.36% while the equal-weight fund RSP rose 0.20% and the health care fund XLV rose 0.54%. Three days is far too short to call that skill.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Technology sold off again. The technology fund XLK fell 2.0% and the chip fund SMH 3.0% on Friday. This morning chip shares fell hard in Asia (Taiwan's index down about 6%, South Korea's about 3.6%), and before the US open Nvidia was down 3% to 4%, AMD and Micron more than 5%. Futures pointed to the S&P 500 opening about 0.6% lower and the Nasdaq 100 about 1.3% lower, with the Dow close to flat. That pattern, giants down and the rest steady, is the one this account is positioned for.
- Nvidia reports after the market closes on Tuesday 17 November, with its finance chief as interim chief executive. The Financial Times reported that the former chief executive has discussed returning; the company has not confirmed it and there is no sign the board has decided anything. The shares are about a third below their early October high.
- Long-term interest rates are still high. The 10-year Treasury yield was quoted near 5.15% this morning. Friday's wholesale price report was mixed: the headline rose 0.3% against 0.4% expected, but the measure without food and energy rose 0.5% against 0.3% expected. Markets still expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates on 9 December. The Fed chair speaks today and the notes of the October meeting come out this week.
- Oil fell (Brent near $93 to $94, US crude near $87) after the International Energy Agency said supply now exceeds demand for the first time since the Iran war began. Lower oil eases inflation a little, though Iran struck a US base in Bahrain on Sunday, so that can reverse.
- A very large new share listing, Anthropic's, is due to price on Wednesday and trade on Thursday. Offerings of that size can pull money out of other technology shares for a few days. It is one more reason the next three days are unusually uncertain for the largest stocks.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it, and whether I would buy it today:

1. SPY ended Friday at $754.37. I cut it if it ends a day below its 200-day average, now about $731.90. It is 3.1% above that, and a 0.6% lower open would still leave it about 2.5% above. It is below its 20-day ($759) and 50-day ($764) averages, so the short-term direction is down while the long rise is intact. Keep; I would still want a broad core here today.

2. RSP ended at $221.16, above its 20, 50 and 200-day averages, and 2.9% above the 50-day average (about $215) that would send it back into SPY. Over 20 trading days it is up 3.3% while SPY is down 1.2%, and the reason for owning it, less riding on the giant technology companies, is exactly what is working. The weak spot remains interest rates: the small-company fund IWM is below all three of its averages, and RSP holds more mid-sized, rate-sensitive companies than SPY. Keep.

3. XLV ended at $188.85, about 0.8% below what I paid, 7.9% above its 50-day average (about $175) and nowhere near the 8% loss limit. I found no new policy news on drug prices or insurance. It is 18% above its 200-day average, which is stretched, so I would not add to it at this price, but nothing says sell. Keep.

4. Cash, $249 (25%). The end date has not changed: fully invested no later than the first trading day after the Federal Reserve decision of 9 December, and sooner if Nvidia's results pass and SPY is back above its 50-day average (about $764). I looked hard at spending some today, since the plan treats cash as a bet against the benchmark. I decided against it for one more day because the single largest known risk lands tomorrow evening, the price of waiting 24 hours is small, and anything bought this morning would be bought into a market that is still selling the stocks that dominate SPY. Wednesday morning's decision will have the results in hand. If they are taken well, the likely move is to put most of the cash into SPY; if they are taken badly and SPY nears its 200-day average, the cash is what lets this account buy lower or simply lose less.

I also considered adding a bank fund (XLF, up 5.7% in 20 days) or a consumer staples fund (XLP, up 5.4%). Both are rising, but both are already inside RSP, staples in particular have run far above their averages, and a fourth line bought the day before the week's main event is not worth the trading cost.
risks: If Nvidia's results are well received, or its former chief executive returns, technology could rebound sharply and the benchmark would beat this account, which holds less technology and keeps a quarter in cash. If long-term interest rates keep climbing or the Fed chair sounds tougher than expected today, RSP is likely to fall more than SPY and could drop to its 50-day average quickly. Health care has risen a long way and could give back several percent if money sheltering there moves on. A sharp fall in the largest stocks could take SPY to its 200-day average within a few days, which would force a sale of the core at a poor price. The futures and pre-market figures quoted here are from before the open and can change by the end of the day; I could not read one of the pre-market news pages, so individual company news may be missing.

summary: No orders today: the account stays entirely in cash because bitcoin spent the day flat between about $63,800 and $65,400, still far below all of its averages, and none of my conditions for buying back has been met.
thesis:
Where the account stands. The account is $988.30 in cash and holds no coins, about 1.2% below its $1,000 start. A plain $1,000 bitcoin holding bought on 11 November was worth $883.50 at the end of 15 November, so the account is about $105 ahead of simply holding bitcoin. All of that lead comes from having been out of the market since 14 November.

What happened. Bitcoin's last price of 15 November was $65,315, up 1.9% on the day after Sunday's brief drop to about $62,000. On 16 November it did very little: reports through the day put it between roughly $63,800 and $65,400, and near $64,600 to $64,800 in the mid-afternoon UTC, a little under where the day began. Ether was around $1,800 to $1,830, Solana about $71 and XRP about $0.96. This calm came on a poor day for shares: by mid-afternoon UTC the Nasdaq was down about 2% and the S&P 500 about 1.2%, with Asian markets down more sharply overnight, and shares of crypto-linked companies such as Coinbase and Strategy down 6% to 7%. Bitcoin holding steady while shares fell is mildly encouraging, since it has moved closely with technology shares over the past month, but one quiet day is not a change of direction.

The trend. Using the figures collected for this account, bitcoin at about $64,700 is roughly 14% below its 20-day average ($75,062), 19% below its 50-day average ($79,756) and 11% below its 200-day average ($72,921). It is down about 18% over 20 days. Every coin on the watch list is below all three of its own averages, and each has fallen about as much as bitcoin or more over 20 days: ether 21%, Solana 28%, XRP 25%. Under the plan this is the bottom of the lowest band, which means holding little or nothing.

The background. US spot bitcoin funds have had seven straight trading days of withdrawals through 13 November, about $1.9 billion in all, with no day of net buying so far this month; ether funds lost about $400 million last week. Monday's fund figures come out on Tuesday. The dollar is at its strongest since April 2025, short-term US government bond yields had their sharpest weekly rise in more than two years, and Federal Reserve officials spoke over the weekend about further rate increases, so markets still expect a rise on 9 December. The Federal Reserve chair gave opening remarks at a conference today; I could not find a reliable account of what he said before making this decision, and the steady bitcoin price afterwards suggests it did not change the picture. None of the pressures behind this fall has eased.

The case for buying, taken seriously. The Fear and Greed index is at 10 for a second day, its lowest since June. About $2 billion of borrowed bets were forcibly closed over the weekend, so much of the forced selling may be behind us. Measures of how stretched the fall has become are at extremes that have often come before a bounce. And bitcoin has now held above Sunday's low for nearly two days, including through a weak day for shares. A relief rally from here is quite possible. Against that: the price is still below the very long-term 200-week average near $67,800 that it lost on Saturday, it has not even managed a day above Sunday's high near $66,000, the funds are still losing money, and the events most likely to move prices this week have not happened yet. This plan buys once the price has turned, not while it is sitting still at the bottom of a fall. The account's lead over the benchmark is large enough that being a little late costs less than being early again, as it was on 12 November.

No other coin earns a place. None has news of its own that outweighs the trend, and Solana funds have reportedly seen six weeks of withdrawals.

What would bring me back, unchanged. I will buy bitcoin again if it ends a UTC day back above its 200-day average, near $73,000, or earlier with a smaller amount if it holds above $70,000 for two UTC days while the bitcoin funds start taking in money again. A return above the 200-week average near $67,800 that lasts would be an early sign the fall is ending, though not enough alone to buy. Below here the levels others are watching are about $62,000 (Sunday's low), $60,000 and the low of 1 July, in the high $50,000s, the lowest of 2026. A lower price by itself is not a reason to buy. This view is wrong if bitcoin rebounds quickly from here: the account would then give back part of its lead over simply holding bitcoin and would buy back at a higher price.

Still to come this week: Monday's bitcoin fund figures and Nvidia's results on Tuesday, and the notes of the Federal Reserve's October meeting on Wednesday.
risks: The main risk is missing a rebound. Fear is extreme, a great deal of forced selling has already happened, and my conditions mean I would buy back 8% to 13% above today's price, so a fast recovery would hand back part of the account's lead over simply holding bitcoin. A slow recovery that never gives a clean signal could do the same over a longer time. My buy-back levels are fixed prices while the averages behind them are falling (the 200-day average has slipped from about $73,100 to $72,900 in a week), so I need to keep checking that they still describe the trend. Today's prices come from news reports published at different times of day, the latest from about 16:35 UTC; I could not get a reading for the final hours before this decision, nor a reliable account of the Federal Reserve chair's remarks or the final level of US shares. Nvidia's results and the Federal Reserve notes could move prices sharply in either direction.

summary: No new orders: all three holdings are still inside the limits set when they were bought, and the $249 in cash waits until Wednesday morning, when Nvidia's results (due after tonight's close) will be known; the S&P 500 fund is now only about 1% above the level at which I would cut it.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Monday 16 November it was worth $986.41 against $973.86 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund. Monday was a bad day for the market: the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 1.91%, the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ 2.67% and the chip fund SMH 5.11%. This account lost less because a quarter of it is in cash and the rest leans away from the giant technology companies: the equal-weight fund RSP fell 1.01% and the health care fund XLV 0.51%. The lead over the benchmark, about $12.50, comes almost entirely from that positioning during a technology sell-off. Four trading days is too short to call it skill.

What has happened since the last decision:

- The technology sell-off deepened. Nvidia fell about 4%, Micron and Intel about 7%. Besides the leadership upheaval at Nvidia, the Commerce Department issued a rule limiting remote access to advanced chips through data centres abroad, and a Singapore-based Nvidia customer was named as having been placed on a no-sell list over suspected diversion of chips to China.
- Factory data were weak: the New York Fed's survey of manufacturers fell to 7.8 in November against 16.7 expected, though it still points to growth. The market's fear gauge, the VIX, rose to about 24.
- Consumer staples were the only S&P 500 sector to rise on Monday. Banks fell more than 2%.
- This morning, before the open, futures pointed to the S&P 500 about 0.3% lower and the Dow about 0.4% to 0.5% lower, with the Nasdaq 100 quoted anywhere from 0.3% lower to 0.3% higher. The 10-year Treasury yield was near 5.12%, a little lower than Monday. Oil was steady, Brent near $93. October retail sales and import prices are published at 8:30 a.m. New York time, after this was written.
- Nvidia reports after tonight's close. Analysts expect revenue of about $109 billion and earnings of about $2.47 a share; options prices imply a move of roughly 4.5% either way. It is the first report without its long-time chief executive.
- Markets still expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates on 9 December.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it, and whether I would buy it today:

1. SPY ended Monday at $739.95. I cut it if it ends a day below its 200-day average, now about $732.16. It is 1.1% above that. It is well below its 20-day ($757.69) and 50-day ($763.82) averages, so the short-term direction is clearly down. The long rise is still intact by the measure I set, so the rule says keep. I am not moving the line to make it easier or harder: if SPY ends a day below about $732, the next decision sells it. What I would then do with the money (move it into RSP, which holds the same companies with far less in the giants, or hold it as cash) depends on why it broke.

2. RSP ended at $218.93, right on its 20-day average and 1.8% above its 50-day average (about $214.98), the level that would send it back into SPY. Over 20 trading days it is up 2.6% while SPY is down 3.5%, so the reason for owning it is still working. It is closer to its limit than it was on Friday, because the selling spread to banks and mid-sized companies on Monday. Keep.

3. XLV ended at $187.88, about 1.4% below what I paid, 7.1% above its 50-day average (about $175.40) and far from the 8% loss limit. Monday's health care news was about single drug companies' trial results, not drug pricing or insurance policy. It is still stretched, 17% above its 200-day average, so I would not add to it, but nothing says sell. Keep.

4. Cash, $249 (25%). The end date is unchanged: fully invested no later than the first trading day after the Fed decision of 9 December, and sooner if Nvidia's results pass and SPY is back above its 50-day average (about $764). Neither condition is met. Any order placed now fills at this morning's open, still before the results, so spending the cash today would give up the one thing waiting was for. Tomorrow's decision will have the results and the market's first reaction to them. If they are taken well, the likely move is to put most of the cash into SPY even if it is not yet back above its 50-day average, because the plan treats cash as a bet against the benchmark and the main reason for holding it will have passed. If they are taken badly and SPY breaks its 200-day average, the cash limits the damage.

I looked again at consumer staples (XLP, up 6.2% in 20 days and the only sector up on Monday) and utilities (XLU, up 6.7%) as shelter. Both are already inside RSP, both are well above their averages after a fast rise, and buying a defensive fund the morning before the event that could reverse the whole pattern is not worth two rounds of fees.
risks: If Nvidia's results are well received, technology could rebound sharply and the benchmark would beat this account, which holds less technology and keeps a quarter in cash. If they are badly received, SPY could fall through its 200-day average within a day or two and this account would sell its core at a poor price. RSP is now within 2% of its own limit, and the selling has started to reach banks and mid-sized companies, so a broad fall would hit it too. Health care has risen a long way and could give back several percent if money sheltering there moves on. Today's retail sales figures, published after this was written, could move interest rates and the market. Several news pages could not be read in full this morning, and the pre-market figures quoted can change by the open.
